sections.h2: Ways to sell a Green Bay house quickly
sections.html:
In Green Bay you may hire an agent, handle the sale yourself, or take cash from a buyer. Cash tends to be fastest, since no bank stands between you and closing day. What suits you depends on the house's condition, whether tenants live in it, and how close the next payment or move is.

  • Listing: the usual choice for a house that looks good, reaching the most buyers but taking the most time.
  • Selling by owner: you keep control of the price and showings, and you also write the contract and complete the disclosures.
  • Cash offer: made for estates, rentals with tenants, houses with code or repair problems, and owners on a clock.

Green Bay is home to about 106,675 people, and its housing ranges from older streets by the river to newer subdivisions farther out. Cash buyers set a price from condition and location, so gather repair estimates and permit records first.

Green Bay is a large, mid-priced market. The figures below are citywide middles and only loosely predict what your own house will bring.

Around 85.1 percent of people were in the same house a year earlier, a sign of a settled local pool of buyers and renters.

sections.h2: Winter wear on Green Bay houses
sections.html: Winter does the most damage here. January averages 16.6 degrees and 68 days a year stay at or below freezing, which is hard on roofs, furnaces and basements. Hold on to invoices for recent work on them, because inspectors and buyers like proof.

sections.h2: Which Green Bay projects need a permit, and what if I skipped one?
sections.html:
A building permit covers most work that is more than cosmetic, and the city's permit guide sorts the cases. A missing permit can come up in a buyer's or lender's review, so go through your own records first.

  • Permit needed: basement and bathroom alterations, decks, cutting new window or door openings, furnace installs, plumbing and electrical work, structural roofing changes, and swapping a gas water heater for electric or the reverse.
  • No permit needed: new flooring, kitchen cabinet replacement, residential siding, exact window replacement, and a same-type water heater swap.
  • Rental houses: a qualified contractor has to pull the permit and perform the work.

Owner-occupants can pull permits and do the labor themselves. Fences longer than 50 feet and sheds larger than 50 square feet need one, while smaller ones do not, but zoning setbacks apply regardless. Houses in a regulated floodplain may have to supply an itemized list of improvements, and houses in a historic district need a certificate of appropriateness. Inspections and Enforcement, at 920-448-3300, can tell you which rules reach your lot. On one- and two-family jobs, the residential permit page says the city verifies the contractor's state Dwelling Contractor Certification and Qualifier Certification before issuing the permit.

sections.h2: Short-term rental permits when you sell
sections.html:
Selling a house does not carry its short-term rental permit along. The city's rules apply to any stay under 28 consecutive days, and its application page calls the permit non-transferable once the property sells, which means a new owner starts over.

The first application costs $500 and each renewal $250. Permit years run July 1 to June 30, renewals open April 1, and a missed June 30 deadline voids the permit. Applicants provide proof of Brown County room tax registration, a Brown County Health Department inspection report, proof of insurance and a local representative within 30 minutes of the property. Allow up to 14 business days for review.

A house that has hosted guests should come with a note to the buyer about which of these items are up to date. Anyone who plans to keep renting it needs to budget for the fee and the processing time.

sections.h2: What a Green Bay seller must disclose
sections.html:
Under Wisconsin Statutes chapter 709, a person selling a property of up to four units owes the buyer a finished condition report inside 10 days of contract acceptance. Miss that, and the buyer gets a two business day window after the deadline to cancel.

Think of the report as a disclosure, not a guarantee. A defect, as the form defines it, is a condition that greatly lowers value, seriously harms health or safety, or would cut the premises' expected life if nobody repaired it. Court-appointed fiduciaries who never lived there are excused. Heirs and long-time owners should still read each question and answer only from what they know.

sections.h2: Transfer fee and recording in Brown County
sections.html:
The state fee that the seller pays is 30 cents for every $100 of value, per Wisconsin Statutes 77.22. Bring it, along with the deed and a signed electronic transfer return, when you record.

Green Bay deeds are recorded by the Brown County Register of Deeds. Find the office in the Northern Building, Room 260, 305 E. Walnut Street, or call 920-448-4470. Counter hours for recording are Monday through Thursday, 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., then 7:30 to 10:30 a.m. Friday. Mail goes to P.O. Box 23600, Green Bay, WI 54305-3600. The Brown County treasurer provides the tax numbers your closing agent needs for proration.

Before the first buyer calls, round up a few documents. The most recent tax bill shows what the treasurer will use for proration. Permit records and invoices prove that roofing, furnace or basement work was done properly. For a tenant-occupied house, keep the lease nearby, and for a guest rental, the permit details.

Tour the house with a notepad and record what you know about the roof, foundation, plumbing and wiring, since known defects go on the form. A clear list also lets a cash buyer name a firm price instead of guessing.

No matter who buys, expect this sequence.

  • Deliver the condition report before day 10 ends.
  • Resolve open permits or code orders, or disclose them.
  • Complete the electronic transfer return and keep its receipt.
  • Have the Brown County Register of Deeds record the deed.
  • Pay your loan payoff and your share of taxes from the proceeds.

Cash takes the lender out of the picture, so the schedule hinges on title work and how ready you are. A listing puts tours, an inspection and loan approval ahead of everything else. Write down the date you accept the contract so you can count the 10 days precisely, and keep copies of what you send the buyer along with proof of when you sent it.

faqs.q: Must I make repairs before selling in Green Bay?
faqs.a: Not required. Selling as is works, and cash buyers take houses in their current state. The condition report must still be completed honestly, and open permits or code orders should be cleared up or disclosed.

faqs.q: Does Green Bay require a permit for siding?
faqs.a: Siding on a house is on the city's no-permit list, though structural roofing changes, decks and furnace installs are not. Confirm your project at 920-448-3300.

faqs.q: Can a buyer keep my Green Bay short-term rental permit?
faqs.a: No. Because it cannot be transferred, the buyer must apply on their own and pay the $500 initial fee.

faqs.q: Who pays the Wisconsin transfer fee?
faqs.a: You do, as seller. The rate is 30 cents per $100 of value, and the Brown County Register of Deeds collects it at recording. Transfers by will or descent are among the exemptions.

faqs.q: How long do I have to give the buyer the condition report?
faqs.a: Within 10 days of acceptance. If it is late, the buyer may rescind within two business days afterward and recover deposits.
